rows.why: Staff who use AI output in internal workflows are given the documented knowledge limits of the AI and the conditions outside its intended use.
The benefit of AI in internal workflows is examined with the staff who use it and compared with a human baseline, so reliance on it is weighed against what it adds.
The cost of a wrong or misused AI output in an internal decision (HR, finance, approvals, operations) is examined by likelihood and magnitude, so the high-impact decisions are identified.
rows.review_reason: Folds MAP 5.1, which also asks the likelihood and magnitude of beneficial impacts and learning from past uses and outside feedback; the why covers only the cost of wrong output.

rows.why: The internal decisions and workflows the AI output may drive are scoped and documented, including which are out of bounds.
Defined human oversight steps tell staff when to check, challenge or override AI output before it drives a decision.
The internal workflow is shown to fail safely, with a manual fallback or hand-off to a person, when AI output is wrong, unavailable or beyond its limits.
AI-assisted internal decisions leave an audit trail, and human oversight and overrides are recorded so high-impact decisions can be audited.
Staff have a way to report problems with AI output and to appeal or challenge decisions made on it, and the reports are analysed.
Staff feedback and the frequency of overrides are measured to show whether people rely on AI output too much or too little.
Controls such as business rules, second approval or limits on AI output keep it from driving high-impact internal decisions unchecked.
A procedure exists to respond to and recover from decisions found to rest on wrong or misused AI output.
The AI-driven internal workflow can be suspended or bypassed, with named owners, when its output proves inconsistent with intended use.
Wrong decisions and misuse of AI output are recorded as incidents, communicated to those affected, and followed up.

notes.reason: Appeals against HR or approval decisions made on AI output protect the people affected; the area's impacts (process, data) may be too narrow.

rows.why: It is decided and documented where AI code generation is allowed and where it is not (for example authentication, cryptography or regulated code).
The human review that AI-generated code must pass before it is merged or reaches production is defined, assigned and shown to be followed, with reviewers told that such code can be wrong or insecure.
The libraries, packages and snippets the AI brings into code are inventoried with their source, so made-up or untrusted dependencies can be found.
Dependencies suggested by the AI are checked against approved sources and for known vulnerabilities before they are used.
rows.review_reason: cis_refs LLM-2.6 (runtime libraries like CUDA in model-serving processes), LLM-2.5 (ML framework extension loading) and LLM-7.1 (AI framework vulnerabilities) are about hosting AI runtimes, not dependencies the AI suggests into code; LLM-16.5 is about training data and model weights. Keep only refs that fit, e.g. LLM-16.4.

rows.why: The coding assistant and its output are tested for AI-specific weaknesses: invented or malicious packages being suggested and manipulation through poisoned context.
Use of AI code generation is logged (who, which tool, what was generated and merged) so AI-written code and prompts can be traced.
Secrets, credentials and sensitive data placed in prompts to code assistants are looked for and measured.
There is a procedure to respond when a secret leaks into a prompt or a malicious or invented dependency reaches the code base.
A coding assistant can be switched off or its access revoked quickly, with defined thresholds, when it leaks secrets or keeps suggesting invented or malicious packages.
Incidents and near-misses from AI-generated code or prompt leaks are recorded, reviewed and communicated to those affected.
The intended purpose, the types of customers and the settings and laws the customer-facing AI operates in are understood and documented.
Customers are told what the customer-facing AI cannot do and that answers may be wrong, and the limits of its output are documented for the people who oversee it.
The costs to customers and to the business of wrong, harmful or leaked answers reaching customers are examined and documented.
The scope of what the customer-facing AI may answer or do is narrowed and documented, taking public misuse and abuse into account.
The oversight that catches high-impact answers before or after they reach customers is defined, assessed and documented.
Practices and people are in place to take in customer feedback about negative and unexpected impacts and act on it.
Production behaviour of the customer-facing AI is monitored for abuse patterns, unusual answers and high-impact answers, with alerts.
The customer-facing AI is shown to fail safely when pushed beyond its knowledge limits or abused by the public, by declining, handing over to a person or staying within bounds.
Prompt injection and other abuse by public users is tested against the customer-facing AI, and the results are documented and acted on.
Customer interactions and high-impact answers are logged so they can be audited, and overrides and human review of answers are recorded.
Leaks of personal or confidential data in answers to customers are monitored and examined.
rows.review_reason: LLM-3.14 is about monitoring LLM logs for access to known sensitive data, not leaks in answers shown to customers; it is off-topic for this row (LLM-3.13 DLP on data passing to and from the model fits).

rows.why: Customers can report problems and appeal outcomes, and the reports are counted and fed into evaluation of the application.
Business rules, filters and throttling limit what the customer-facing AI can say or do for the public.
Customer reports of problems and newly found risks are handled through a response and recovery procedure.
The customer-facing AI can be switched off or replaced when answers go wrong, with thresholds and owners defined.
Customer feedback is turned into measurable improvements in each update of the customer-facing AI.
Incidents and errors in front of customers are tracked, communicated to those affected, and reviewed afterwards.

missing.reason: Nothing asks whether post-deployment monitoring of the customer-facing AI is run in practice, including capturing customer input, appeal and override, and change management.
Customer feedback, positive and negative, and how often answers are overridden are not used to check whether the application performs as intended in front of customers.
Nothing checks performance of the customer-facing AI under real public conditions (unexpected, non-optimised use by customers) rather than only lab conditions.
Nothing asks whether the benefits customers are meant to get from the AI are examined, with customer input on perceived benefit, so harms can be weighed against them.

rows.why: The vendor AI features in use and the org data each one processes are identified, with their intended purpose and the settings they run in.

The vendor's model provider, sub-processors, upstream dependencies and external data connections behind each AI feature are documented, with what the vendor states about the feature's limits and intended use.
The risks of each vendor's AI, its model provider, data retention and training use, terms of service, and the vendor's security and tenant isolation are assessed and documented before and during use.
rows.review_reason: Folds MEASURE 2.7 (security and resilience evaluated) but the why only asks the vendor's security and tenant isolation are assessed; resilience (vendor outage, failure of the AI feature) is not asked, and the org cannot red-team a vendor model.

rows.why: Vendor AI behaviour and unannounced feature or model changes are watched in production, not only at onboarding.
Vendor AI activity on org data is traceable through the vendor's own logs or the org's, so data flows to the provider can be reviewed.
The privacy risk of org data flowing to vendor AI, including retention and training use by the provider, is examined and documented.
rows.review_reason: Repeats MAP 4.1 and MANAGE 3.1 (retention and training use by the provider) and overlaps Input (sensitive data sent to a provider); the why is not distinct.

rows.why: The org decides whether each vendor AI feature is worth its data risk and stays enabled, and re-decides when the vendor changes it without notice.
When a new vendor AI risk appears, such as a changed data practice or a vendor-side leak, there is a procedure to respond and recover.
A vendor AI feature can be switched off, or the vendor's access to data revoked, when it behaves outside intended use or terms change.

Each vendor's AI is monitored regularly and the risk controls actually applied are documented, such as training opt-out, history retention off, data minimisation, risky features disabled and which data classes may go to the vendor.
rows.review_reason: Folds MANAGE 2.2 (mechanisms applied to sustain the value of deployed AI) but the why never asks about sustaining value or business rules limiting output; folding MAP 4.2 (controls identified) into a MANAGE row also blurs a MAP check, so MAP 4.2 would be clearer as its own row.

rows.why: Vendor AI incidents and errors are reported between the vendor and the org, tracked, responded to and recorded.

notes.reason: Unannounced vendor feature or model changes also harm the processes relying on the feature; the area's impacts (data only) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Nothing asks which systems, data classes and uses each vendor AI feature is scoped to; this is only buried in MANAGE 3.1's why.

rows.why: Requirements for the model being built (privacy, security, trustworthiness) are gathered from its recipients and put into build and tuning decisions.
The task the org builds or tunes its model for, and the method used (from scratch or tuning an existing model), are defined and documented.
The limits of the model it builds, and the settings outside its intended use, are documented and told to the recipients of each release.
The benefits of building or tuning an own model, compared with using an existing one, are examined and documented before the work is run.
The scope a built model is released for (users, products, regions, uses) is specified and documented, and releases outside it are limited.
Base models, components and third-party data or software used to build or tune are assessed for legal, licence and IP risk before use.
Internal risk controls apply to the base models and components chosen for building, and only approved ones are used.
Build, tuning and release events are logged with who did what, so changes to the model and its releases can be traced and accounted for.
The environmental impact of training and tuning runs is assessed and documented as part of how building is run.
Before a built or tuned version is released, a decision is made on whether it meets its intended purpose and should proceed.
A problem found in a released model is responded to and recovered from by a defined procedure that covers rebuilding or withdrawing it.
rows.review_reason: Its why ends in 'rebuilding or withdrawing it', which repeats the withdrawal check of MANAGE 2.4; keep this row to responding to and recovering from a newly found problem (rebuild, fix, restore) and leave withdrawal to MANAGE 2.4.

rows.why: A release can be withdrawn or superseded, with responsibility assigned and recipients told, when it performs against its intended use.
The pre-trained base models used for building are tracked and monitored, including for published vulnerabilities and upstream changes.
Changes to how the model is built or tuned, and new versions, are managed, reviewed and approved with recipients engaged before release.
Errors and incidents in released models are communicated to recipients, and a record is kept of system changes and why they were made.

notes.reason: Environmental impact of training runs harms the environment and society, not assets; the area's impacts (assets only) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Nothing checks that the model it builds is explained and documented for recipients (model type, training approach, intended uses, thresholds, e.g. a model card shipped with each release); MAP 2.2 covers limits only.
Nothing checks that recipients of a release have a way to report problems with the model and that those reports feed back into building and tuning.

rows.why: The org finds and lists the AI tools, features, PoCs and local models staff use without approval, what data they receive and where it goes, and the outside AI agents connecting in, not only the approved ones.
rows.review_reason: Folds MAP 2.2 (documented knowledge limits and how output is overseen by humans) but the why only asks about finding and listing unapproved tools and agents; that outcome is not asked, so drop the fold.

rows.why: The org has controls that decide which AI services, browser extensions and software are allowed (safelists, DNS and extension limits) and applies them to third-party AI.
The org watches in practice for new unapproved AI use and for outside agents or MCP clients reaching its systems, using network, DNS and provider telemetry with alerts.
The org tests and measures how its systems hold up to outside agents, scrapers and MCP clients acting on behalf of users at machine speed (authentication, throttling, filtering).
Logs record which AI services staff reach and which outside agents or MCP clients call org systems and under whose identity, so activity can be traced and accounted for.
The org checks whether personal, regulated or confidential data is being sent to unapproved AI tools, for example through data loss prevention on AI traffic.
The org has a followed procedure for responding to and recovering from data leaving through unapproved AI or an outside agent misusing access, including how staff report it.
The org can switch off or block an unapproved AI tool or an outside agent or MCP client, and revoke the access it holds, once found.

Risks from AI inside third-party tools and services staff use are monitored, and controls such as blocking, data loss prevention, central sign-in for machine clients and staff training are applied and documented in practice.
rows.review_reason: The why repeats other rows (blocking = MAP 4.2, data loss prevention = MEASURE 2.10, training), and AI inside vendor tools is the vendor_ai area; it also folds MANAGE 2.2 (sustaining the value of deployed AI), which the why never asks and which does not fit this area.

rows.why: Incidents and near-misses from unapproved AI use or outside agents are recorded, communicated to those affected and reviewed afterwards.

missing.reason: Nothing checks that the org assesses likelihood and magnitude of harm from the unapproved AI use and outside agents it finds (what data, how sensitive, how often), which is needed to prioritise treatment.
Nothing checks whether the org understands what benefits staff get from unapproved AI tools and whether approved alternatives meet that need; unmet need is what drives invisible usage.

rows.why: The third-party providers that receive prompts and files are identified, with what their terms say about keeping or reusing that input.
How likely and how serious exposure of data through prompts and files is judged to be, based on what staff and systems actually send and its data class.
Prompts and responses are logged as a record with who sent what, who can read those logs and how long they are kept, so exposure can be traced and accounted for.
rows.review_reason: The why asks how long logs are kept, which MANAGE 4.1 already asks (retention); keep this row to who sent what and who can read the logs.

rows.why: Personal and sensitive data in prompts and files is examined and monitored in production, with alerts when it appears, including data leaving the org and access to the stored prompt and response logs.
rows.review_reason: Folds MEASURE 2.4 but the why only asks for sensitive data monitoring; monitoring what staff and systems send in production (volumes, file types, unexpected input) is not asked, so 2.4 is not fully covered.

rows.why: Controls are applied to what goes into the model, such as removing sensitive data, blocking it, and protecting prompts and logs in transit and at rest.
When sensitive data is found to have been sent to a model or provider, the org follows a procedure to respond, contain and recover.
Sending input to a model or provider can be stopped quickly (blocking the provider, cutting the feed) when sensitive data is found leaving, with defined thresholds and who decides.
Risk controls are applied and monitored for providers that receive the org's prompts and files, including what they keep.
rows.review_reason: Repeats MAP 4.1 (providers receiving prompts and what they keep) and the vendor's model provider handling belongs to vendor_ai; the why is vague and LLM-8.12 (provider logs) does not support it.

rows.why: Retention and deletion of prompt and response logs and of input held by providers are carried out and tracked, including deletion requests.
rows.review_reason: This outcome is post-deployment monitoring, appeal, override and change; retention and deletion of logs is a data control that fits MANAGE 2.2, which already protects prompts and logs.

missing.reason: Nothing checks that exposures of sensitive input are recorded and communicated to the affected people, providers and regulators after they are found.

rows.why: The knowledge limits of the AI's answers, and how people and systems may rely on them, are documented for those who use them.
The cost of wrong, manipulated or biased answers, and who could be harmed by acting on them, is examined and documented.
The AI is limited to the uses and contexts where its answers have been shown trustworthy, and use beyond that scope is restricted.
The likelihood and size of harm from wrong or manipulated answers are assessed, including red teaming for prompt injection and unsafe output.
The test sets, metrics, tools and assumptions used to test answers for accuracy, consistency and bias are defined and documented.
rows.review_reason: Folds MAP 2.3 but the why does not ask experimental design, validity of the tests or how test data was chosen; it only asks that test sets, metrics and tools are documented.

rows.why: The test cases for accuracy and bias match the people and situations actually affected, and gaps between test and real users are analysed.
Answer quality is measured under conditions like real use (real prompts, messy input), not only ideal ones, and the results are kept.
Answer quality and behaviour are monitored in production so drift, anomalies and rising error rates are noticed and alerted.
The AI is shown to give accurate and consistent answers before use, and the conditions beyond which answers cannot be trusted are documented.
The AI is tested to fail safely, for example declining or flagging when it is outside its knowledge limits, rather than giving a confident wrong answer.
Answers are tested against attacker steering such as prompt injection through user input or retrieved content, and the results are documented.
Answers are logged with enough detail to trace how a wrong or manipulated answer came about and who relied on it.
Answers are tested for bias, comparing how people or groups are treated, and the results are documented.
The accuracy, consistency and bias tests are themselves reviewed for whether they actually catch bad answers.
Domain experts and users confirm that answers are valid, reliable and consistent in real use, and how often people override answers is measured.
rows.review_reason: The clause on how often people override answers belongs to Internal process (how staff check, challenge and override); keep only expert and user confirmation of answer validity.

rows.why: Baselines for answer quality are set and improvements or declines over time are identified and documented.
Someone decides from test results whether the answers are good enough for the intended purpose to keep using the AI.
Controls such as business rules and output guardrails limit or restrict what answers can do in certain contexts.
There is a procedure to respond to and recover from a newly found answer problem such as an injection route, a bias or a drift.
Thresholds and owners exist to bypass or switch off the AI when its answers prove inconsistent with intended use.
A post-deployment plan re-tests answers for validity, reliability, bias and security, with red teaming at a set cadence.
Wrong, biased or inconsistent answers lead to measurable fixes (prompts, data, model, rules) that are re-tested.
Wrong, biased or manipulated answers are recorded as errors or incidents, tracked, and shared with those affected.

missing.reason: Nothing asks what the AI's intended purpose and prospective settings are, and what counts as a correct answer for them; accuracy, consistency and bias tests have no stated target without it.

Nothing checks that accuracy, consistency and bias tests are done or reviewed by someone other than the developers (independent assessors, domain experts, affected users); the area includes testing for organisations that build their own model.

rows.why: How training, tuning, evaluation and test sets are collected and selected (availability, representativeness, suitability) is documented, and the harness test cases are kept separate from the data the model was trained on.
The sources of third-party and licensed data used for training, tuning and testing are identified, with the rights and IP or licence risks of using them.
Third-party datasets and feedback or logs reused for tuning are reviewed for bias, privacy and poisoning risk before they enter a training, tuning or test set.
The evaluation and test sets, metrics and harness tools are documented and versioned, so a result can be traced to the exact data and test cases used.
Evaluation sets drawn from people (human-subject data, feedback) meet consent and protection requirements and represent the population the system serves.
Training and tuning sets, the evaluation set and the harness are tested and protected against poisoning and tampering, including changes made to hide failures.
Changes to and access to training, tuning and evaluation data and the harness are logged and attributable to a person, so tampering and misuse can be traced.
Personal and sensitive data in training sets and in feedback or logs reused for tuning is identified, minimised or removed, and its use is documented.
The evaluation set and harness are reviewed to confirm they still catch real failures, are refreshed, and have not been narrowed or leaked into training.
Controls on the data used for training, tuning and testing (quality, minimisation, encryption, retention, deletion on request) are applied in practice.
When poisoned or tampered training, tuning or evaluation data, or a leak from them, is found, the org responds and restores a clean, verified copy of the data and harness.

The legal and IP risks of the model's components are mapped: licence terms and provenance of base models, fine-tuning data and third-party prompts or configurations, and the risk of infringing or leaking rights in the model itself.
rows.review_reason: Licence terms and provenance of base models and fine-tuning data belong to Model building and Test, tuning and evaluation data; the Model area is the weights and versions as IP, so the why mixes in other areas' checks.

rows.why: Internal controls that protect the model artifacts (storage, access, versioning, release of weights) are identified and documented.
rows.review_reason: Repeats MANAGE 2.2 (controls on weights, versions, prompts) in different words, and only asks that controls are identified and documented; LLM-3.3 is about retrieved content and memory stores (Source data), off-topic here.

rows.why: API usage and version state are monitored in production for signs of model extraction, copying or unexpected changes to a deployed version.
The model is tested for theft, extraction through the API and tampering with versions, and the results are documented.
Access to weights, prompts and configurations, and changes to model versions, are logged so copying or tampering can be traced to who did it.
rows.review_reason: LLM-3.14 (monitor LLM logging for access to known sensitive data) does not support logging access to weights, prompts and version changes; LLM-8.5 is mostly about user inputs and outputs (Input area); LLM-8.1 or LLM-8.10 would fit better.

rows.why: Controls such as restricted access, encryption and protected backups are applied to weights, fine-tuned versions and system prompts.
rows.review_reason: LLM-3.3 is about retrieved content and memory stores (Source data), off-topic for protecting weights; LLM-6.8 (role separation for model promotion) or LLM-6.5 (MFA on model registries) would support it.

rows.why: Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover from theft, leakage or tampering of the model or its configuration.
A tampered or leaked model version can be withdrawn, rolled back to a trusted version, and access to it revoked.
What the retrieval store covers and does not cover, and the upstream data the AI depends on, is documented so users and assessors know what answers can rest on it.
rows.review_reason: Subcategory is knowledge limits and human oversight of output; the why (coverage plus upstream data) repeats MAP 4.1's source identification, with the same CIS refs LLM-3.2 and LLM-3.8.

rows.why: What content is collected into the retrieval store and how it is selected for suitability, quality and trustworthiness of source is defined and documented.
The sources feeding the retrieval store, including third-party or external content, are identified with where the data flows and the rights to use it.
Controls on the store itself are identified and documented: classification of its content, who can read or change it, and protection against tampering.
The content of the store and the answers drawn from it are monitored in production for unexpected changes, poisoned or stale material.
Retrieval permissions, poisoning and copying out of the store through the AI are tested, so users only see what they are entitled to.
Retrievals and changes to the store are logged with who asked and what was returned, so access to sensitive content can be traced.
Personal and sensitive data held in the store is identified, classified and checked for exposure through the AI.
Store content is kept current and accurate, and outdated or no longer needed material is retired or securely disposed of.
Procedures exist to respond to and recover from poisoned or leaked store content, including cleaning the store and re-indexing.
rows.review_reason: The why asks whether procedures 'exist' (a GOVERN-style existence check) rather than what is done in practice when store content is found poisoned or leaked.

rows.why: A source or the whole store can be disconnected from retrieval quickly when it is found poisoned or over-exposed, with responsibility assigned.
Changes to the store after go-live are tracked, and deletion and rectification requests reach the store and its index so removed content stops being retrieved.

notes.reason: Stale or poisoned content makes answers wrong and harms decisions and processes using them; the area's impacts (data, access) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Requirements for the store (who may see which content through the AI, privacy and entitlement expectations) are not asked anywhere; this is where retrieval entitlements are set.
Nothing checks that third-party or external content feeding the store is monitored and its risks controlled over time; MAP 4.1 only covers identification.
Nothing checks that retrieval fails safely, for example refusing rather than exposing restricted content when permission or classification checks fail or the store misbehaves.

rows.why: The outside networks, servers and upstream systems the AI's tools connect to, and how data flows to them, are documented.
The scope of what each tool can read, write and do, and the credentials it uses, is specified against what the use case needs.
The tools and MCP servers the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are identified with who runs each and what third-party software it brings.
Internal controls for each tool or MCP server (approval before use, permission limits, allowed versions) are identified and documented.
rows.review_reason: The why's 'permission limits' repeats MAP 3.3 (scope and credentials) and MANAGE 2.2 (permissions kept within bounds), and MCP-6.8 is reused in all three; narrow it to approval before use and allowed versions.

rows.why: The likelihood and size of harm from tool misuse (injected instructions, over-broad permissions, a compromised outside server) are assessed.
Tool use in production is monitored for unexpected calls, new capabilities on a known server and unusual volume.
Tools and MCP servers are tested for security, including prompt injection driving tool calls, permission abuse and a malicious or changed server.
Tool calls are logged with the credentials used and what was done, so actions can be traced and accounted for.
The privacy risk of data flowing through tools to MCP servers and outside services is examined, including what leaves and to whom.
Controls that keep tool use within bounds in practice (permissions narrower than the user's, short-lived credentials, gateway enforcement, rate limits) are applied and kept working.
A tool or MCP incident (misused credential, injected call, compromised server) has a response and recovery procedure that is followed.
A tool, credential or MCP server can be switched off or revoked quickly, with an owner assigned, when it misbehaves.
Outside MCP servers and tool suppliers are monitored regularly and their risk controls applied and documented.
Post-deployment monitoring of tools covers change management for new tools or permissions, review of use, and decommissioning of unused tools.
rows.review_reason: 'Review of use' repeats the MEASURE 2.4 check on production tool use (same MCP-8.11); keep only change management for new tools or permissions and decommissioning.

rows.why: Tool incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected, and followed up after recovery.

missing.reason: Nothing asks which tool actions (writes, deletes, payments, external sends) need a human to confirm before they run; MCP-17.4 itself mentions human confirmation enforcement.
Nothing checks that the AI fails safely when a tool or MCP server errors, times out, is unavailable or returns something unexpected, rather than retrying or taking partial changes.

rows.why: The tasks each agent performs and the chains of actions, tools and systems it uses to do them are defined and documented.
The agent's knowledge limits, the conditions outside its intended use, and how its output is used and overseen by humans are documented.
The scope of what each agent may do on its own is specified: which systems, which actions, which data, and which actions are never left to it.
Human oversight of agent actions is defined: which steps need approval or review, who does it, and how it is trained and assessed.

The components an agent is built on (models, orchestration frameworks, libraries, executors) are identified and held to approved, controlled versions, with their legal and supply-chain risks documented.
rows.review_reason: Folded MAP 4.1 is not fully asked: the why says 'legal and supply-chain risks documented' but not third-party IP/rights infringement or the inventory of third-party material; AGENT-16.4 (third-party component inventory) supports it and is missing.

rows.why: The likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions are assessed, including irreversible changes and actions triggered by manipulated input.
rows.review_reason: AGENT-16.6 is a vulnerability severity rating process, not evidence for likelihood and magnitude of harm from agent actions; drop it.

rows.why: Agent behaviour in production is monitored for unexpected action chains, tool use and drift from what was approved.
The agent is shown to complete its tasks correctly and reliably under realistic conditions, and the limits of where it can be trusted are documented.
rows.review_reason: Showing the agent answers correctly and reliably is accuracy/consistency TEVV, done at Output for everyone; keep only if reworded to agent task completion and limits of autonomy; empty cis_refs although AGENT-16.13 (evaluation harnesses, adversarial inputs) supports it.

rows.why: Agents are tested under stress and unexpected conditions to show they fail safely, with loops and runaway action chains stopped.
Agent security is tested with adversarial and red-team exercises, including manipulated input that triggers actions and attempts to break out of the sandbox.
Agent actions, tool calls and the identity used are logged and kept so what an agent did can be traced and reviewed.
An agent's decisions and action chains can be explained, documented and interpreted in context, so reviewers understand why it acted.
rows.review_reason: Largely repeats MEASURE 2.8 (what the agent did, traced from logs); AGENT-8.5/8.11 are the same evidence; no distinct explainability check for this area.

rows.why: Privacy risk from the data an agent reads, keeps in memory and passes between tools is examined, including redaction in logs.
rows.review_reason: Redaction in logs and the log CIS refs (AGENT-8.1, 8.5) belong to Input (prompt and response logs); privacy of data passed between tools overlaps Input, Source data and MCP/tools; the row reads as generic privacy.

rows.why: Staff and others can report agent misbehaviour and unexpected actions, and these reports feed how the agent is evaluated.
Feedback from operators and users, and how often staff override the agent, are used to judge whether it performs as intended.
Results are used to decide whether the agent achieves its purpose and whether its autonomy should continue, be reduced or be stopped.
Controls limit what an agent can do: least-privilege identities, sandboxing, approval for high-impact or irreversible steps, and limits on rate and cost.
Agent-specific incidents are responded to and recovered from, including reversing the changes an agent made.
An agent can be stopped, bypassed or its access revoked quickly when it acts outside its intended use, and who may do so is assigned.
Post-deployment monitoring of agents covers staff override, change management of agent configuration and tools, and retirement of agents.
rows.review_reason: Staff override is the same check as MEASURE 4.2 (override frequency); the why also mixes change management and retirement, so it asks several things; AGENT-8.11 log review does not support override.

rows.why: Agent incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected and reviewed for root cause.

notes.reason: The row limits rate and cost, which harms spend/assets; the area's impacts (access, process, data) may be too narrow.

missing.reason: Nothing checks agent performance and assurance criteria measured under conditions like the real deployment (real systems, messy inputs, non-optimised conditions); AGENT-16.13 supports it.
Nothing asks what benefit justifies giving the agent autonomy (time saved, error rates against a human baseline) as examined with its users.

rows.why: The hosting environment's dependencies and connections to external networks and the internet (serving endpoints, registries, providers) are documented.
The costs of a hosting compromise, outage or cost abuse (stolen compute, runaway spend, downtime) are examined and tied to risk tolerance.
The servers, GPUs, registries, serving software and third-party hosting material the org relies on are inventoried and their risks mapped.
Third-party hosting material (base images, serving software, models and packages pulled from registries, provider services) is reviewed for security vulnerabilities and approved before it is used.
The likelihood and magnitude of hosting compromise, outage and cost abuse are assessed, drawing on past incidents and provider reports, to prioritise treatment.
Hosts and serving endpoints are monitored in production for anomalies such as unusual load, cost spikes, configuration changes or tampering.
The hosted service is tested to fail safely and recover under high load, resource exhaustion and component failure.
Security and resilience of the hosting environment and exposed endpoints are tested through vulnerability scans and adversarial exercises.
Administrative, registry, secret-access and endpoint activity on the hosting environment is logged so actions can be traced and accounted for.
Controls that sustain the hosted service (authenticated access, network isolation, throttling, firewalling) are in place and applied.
rows.review_reason: Why leaves out secrets, keys and the model registry, which the area covers, and cis_refs omit LLM-4.6 (centralised, scoped secret management) and LLM-4.1 (hardened serving configuration), which support it.

rows.why: Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover hosting from compromise, outage or abuse, including restoring from backups.
